source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration? (accepted CogSci 2026)
finding: Adults tested on a blicket-style task (called 'nexiom') with self-chosen tests. The paper says it is accepted at CogSci 2026, so a peer-reviewed form of the earlier preprint now exists. Adults need more tests for the AND rule than the OR rule. Self-directed testing helped; planning tests without seeing the results hurt.
numbers: N=306 adults on Prolific, 102 per condition (active, passive observer, passive proposer). 4 objects, so 32 hypotheses (2^(n+1)). Tests: AND mean 9.6 vs OR 6.4. AND object identification: active 0.69, passive observer 0.45, passive proposer 0.12. Average adult AND errors: 16% wrong on both rule and objects, 16% right rule but wrong objects.
quote: Active intervention alone is insufficient: effective causal learning requires adaptive search strategies and progressive hypothesis pruning
limits: Adults only. No children tested with active exploration, so the child-vs-adult question under active exploration is still open. Rule-by-condition cell sizes are garbled in the text (about 51 per rule). Online sample.
agent_relevance: Planning a test without seeing its outcome was worse than just watching, so a REVISE step should run on the agent's own test results, not on a plan written ahead of the data.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) LLM arm of the same study (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o4-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, deepseek-chat)
finding: With active exploration, reasoning models close much of the AND/OR gap that older models showed. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner reach near-perfect or perfect full-hypothesis accuracy on OR. On AND, strong reasoning models are far more robust than deepseek-chat and o4-mini, but still below top humans. The AND task needs longer test sequences for models as for people.
numbers: 6 LLMs, same Nexiom task, 4 objects, 32 hypotheses. OR: gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner match top humans. AND: average adults beat most models; deepseek-chat and o4-mini only modestly above the random baseline; gpt-5 and gpt-5-mini more robust; top humans 100%. Exact per-model AND numbers are only in a figure and were not read.
limits: Small number of trials per model (figure-only numbers). 4 objects only. Text interface. Answers gap 2 only in part: reasoning models are better, but the paper does not separate hypothesis-space size from prior bias.
agent_relevance: Test the schema on current reasoning models, not 2023-2025 non-reasoning ones. The AND handicap shrinks with reasoning, so gains from scaffolding may shrink too.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Re-read for gap 2. Four findings. (1) The InfoGain oracle solves every AND and OR case (accuracy 1), so the AND handicap is the agent, not the task. (2) o3-mini and o4-mini with HIGHER reasoning effort lag lower-effort variants and the oracle on 8-object AND exploration. (3) Longer responses correlate with lower accuracy (p<0.05); taking more steps also correlates negatively with success. (4) Sampling more unique hypotheses to build a flatter prior removes the AND/OR gap. The authors offer two guesses for (2): reasoning amplifies the disjunctive prior, or the models overfit to verifiable tasks.
numbers: At least 16 independent trials per model, prompt and system-message cell. All LMs fall when objects go from 4 to 8, and when OR goes to AND. Oracle accuracy 1.0.
limits: The hypothesis-sampling fix changes hypothesis-space size and prior flatness at the same time (more unique samples = bigger and flatter pool), so this paper cannot separate the two causes. Models are 2025 era (gpt-4o, o3-mini, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Text only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open on cause. The fix works, so seeding O1 with a large enumerated hypothesis pool is cheap to try. Do not assume more thinking tokens help on AND-type tasks.

source: Gopnik, Griffiths, Lucas et al. (2017) Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history from childhood to adolescence to adulthood (PNAS)
finding: Original numbers for the age curve behind the 'child better than adult' claim. In the AND (conjunctive) condition, the share calling the ambiguous object D a blicket falls with age: 4-year-olds 0.92, 6-7 0.56, 9-11 0.60, 12-14 0.28, adults 0.25. Adolescents and adults look alike and are less flexible than young children. In the social-attribution task the pattern is an inverted U: 12-14-year-olds were more flexible than 6-year-olds and adults.
numbers: Exp 1: new samples 6-7 (n=90), 9-11 (n=90), 12-14 (n=86); 4-year-olds and adults taken from Lucas et al. 2014 (n not given in the text read). Pooled D judgments: AND 0.52, OR 0.13, baseline 0.15. Fisher exact (AND): 4 vs 6-7 P<0.01; 6-7 and 9-11 vs 12-14 P<0.05 each; 12-14 vs adults P=1.0. Exp 2: 240 adults on Mechanical Turk; baseline situation-attribution 4-year-olds 0.93 vs 12-14 0.24 (P=0.001) and adults 0.38 (P=0.004).
limits: Passive evidence design (people watch a fixed sequence). Four-year-olds and adults reused from a 2014 paper. Mostly post-hoc tests. Adults tested online, children in person. The Lucas replication in low-SES preschoolers is only a footnote to a conference talk. The text flags a possible t-value typo.
agent_relevance: The 'broad hypothesis' advantage of children is a prior effect on the unlikely rule. Samiei 2026 shows adults do fine with active testing, so do not copy a child-like prior into the schema; copy the active-testing loop.

source: Bonawitz, Shafto, Gweon, Goodman, Spelke, Schulz (2011) The double-edged sword of pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery (Cognition)
finding: Original numbers for gap 9. After a teacher demonstrates one function of a toy as a teaching act, preschoolers play less, try fewer kinds of actions, focus on the shown function, and find fewer of the hidden functions. The same demonstration done by accident or interrupted narrows search less. In Exp 2, an adult who is learning too (intentional) kept exploration broader than a direct teaching demonstration.
numbers: Exp 1 N=85 preschoolers, mean age 58 months (48-72): Pedagogical n=25, Interrupted/Naive/Baseline n=20 each. Playtime in seconds (Pedagogical/Interrupted/Naive/Baseline): 119.2 / 179.6 / 132.7 / 205.7, F(1,81)=4.52 p<.05. Action kinds, full play: 4.00 / 5.30 / 5.90 / 6.15, F(1,81)=9.39 p<.01. Share of play on the shown squeaker: 0.68 / 0.53 / 0.38. Hidden functions found (0-3): 0.72 / 1.3 / 1.2 / 1.15, F(1,81)=4.58 p<.05. Exp 2 N=64 (mean age 61 months): hidden functions Direct 0.50, Indirect child 0.75, Indirect adult 1.31, Intentional 1.00, F(1,60)=6.38 p<.05.
limits: Preschoolers and one toy design. Planned contrasts pooled across conditions, not each pair. Exp 2 per-cell n not reported. Narrowing costs discovery of other functions but helps learning of the shown one (a trade-off, not only a harm). The page read gives two experiments.
agent_relevance: Confirms the effect size behind K15. Open point: whether a directive system prompt narrows an LLM agent's search the same way. No LLM test found (see d17).

source: Perez and Derex (2026) Socially guided individual learning mitigates the double-edged sword of pedagogy (Proc. R. Soc. B 293)
finding: A pre-registered adult study that extends the pedagogy narrowing idea. Learners who inherited a heuristic explored more often and more broadly than learners who inherited a finished solution. Both groups still beat their demonstrator.
numbers: 400 adult participants, pre-registered. Only the abstract was read, through the Europe PMC record; no cell sizes or statistics seen. The PMC page itself was blocked by a browser check.
limits: Abstract only (opened false). Adults, a problem-solving task, not a causal-learning task. A conceptual extension, not a replication of the preschool design.
agent_relevance: Hand the agent a heuristic or a goal, not a worked plan, when you want broad search. An analogue for system prompts, but only in humans so far.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Resolves the open contradiction between earlier evidence lines. Wason rule discovery (11 LLMs, 45-turn cap): thinking-mode Qwen3-8B success 0.21 to 0.36 with Think-in-Opposites (TiO), Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.61. Blicket test (192 episodes, AND/OR/XOR, 4 or 8 objects): Qwen3-8B 0.32 to 0.40, Qwen3-32B 0.57 to 0.86; non-thinking Qwen3-8B 0.11 to 0.19. So 0.21-0.36 is Wason and 0.32-0.40 is blicket; the earlier '0.21 to 0.40' mixed the two. Average over all models: success 42% to 56%. Gains are significant for thinking models and small or mixed for non-thinking models. Switching non-thinking to thinking raises success without a consistent rise in I:C.
numbers: Human baseline from Wason: 29 people, 21 found the rule; mean I:C 1.79 for first-guess correct vs 0.24 for first-guess wrong. LLM: I:C vs success correlation significant in both thinking and non-thinking. Blicket I:C base to TiO: 8B 0.44 to 0.57, 32B 0.54 to 1.31. Tokens per turn: non-thinking up to 256, thinking up to 16K. Dual-Goal helped in 8 of 11 model-inference setups, TiO in all 11. Distilling TiO from Wason into the student raised blicket success but stayed below TiO prompting.
limits: One lab, one main model family (Qwen3) plus Gemini-2.5-Pro and others. TiO and baseline are not token-matched. Blicket is a transfer test of 192 episodes. Preprint.
agent_relevance: The I:C ratio is cheap to log at S5. Counterexample prompts work where the model already thinks; they are weak on non-thinking models, so test the schema on a thinking model.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FALSIFYBENCH: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: A different lab and a semantic (WordNet) version of the Wason game. It confirms the link between negative testing and success, but only as a correlation, not as a prompt intervention. Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones; small reasoning models do not. Failed games show MORE confirmation bias than won games for the same model.
numbers: 12 LLMs x 100 games = 1,200 games. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Spearman rho = -0.779 (p=0.003) between confirmation bias and success. Mixed-effects odds ratio 0.016 across the full bias range (about 1/63 the odds). Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%. GPT-5.2-Chat bias 20% in won vs 50% in lost games.
limits: Correlational. Only one test turn and one guess turn per game were human-checked for oracle errors. The dominant configuration is hypothesis inside target, so it measures one case of the Klayman-Ha analysis. It cites Jhaveri but does not replicate its intervention.
agent_relevance: Independent support for logging a 'tests outside current hypothesis' rate at S5 as a health signal. Does not show that prompting it works outside the Jhaveri lab.

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu, Xing (2026) Separable Pathways for Causal Reasoning (Amigo AI, under review) - boundary conditions re-read
finding: Re-read for gaps 3 and 8. The scaffold helps only where the hypothesis space must be restructured. With a noisy machine (conjunctive rule, activation probability 0.70) all three agents land at 73-77% and the scaffold adds nothing, even though the stochasticity monitor fired in 77% of episodes: the agent noticed noise but could not tell a true cause that failed from a non-cause. Order-sensitive rules: 30% vs 20%, p=0.276. The within-lab replication holds: CG+DB over CG +16.6 pp (Run 03), +16.7 (Run 04, independent seed, pre-registered), +6.0 (Run 06).
numbers: Hidden-moderator easy raw accuracy: Base 87.3%, CG 77.3%, CG+DB 89.1% (p=0.015). Hard reasoning-eligible accuracy: 73.3%, 93.9%, 95.3% (p=0.038). Stochastic p=0.70: 76.7%, 76.7%, 73.3%, n=30 each. 1,085 episodes in the main series cost about $807 in API fees; full program 2,541 episodes about $1,950.
limits: All on Claude Sonnet 4.5 plus Haiku 4.5 for monitors; no cross-model run (the authors list this as a limit). Dynamic behaviours are hand-written by the authors. Monitor cost is not matched against baselines. Synthetic blicket world.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 half answered: noisy machines erase the scaffold gain in this company-lab scaffold. Gap 3 stays open: no outside lab has repeated this. Add a repeat-the-same-test statistics step before relying on REVISE in noisy tasks.

source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B
finding: Closest direct answer to gap 1, though not on blicket tasks. When every method is charged for every token it writes (critiques, reflections, debate turns), nothing beats plain repeated sampling with majority vote. All methods in which the model inspects or rewrites its own output do worse. At 7B, Self-Refine is still below the equal-cost baseline by 3.6 to 10.1 points.
numbers: Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B, 7B; GSM8K and MATH-500; 150 questions each; 7 methods; 36 comparisons. After Holm correction: 0 better, 10 worse, 26 not distinguishable; 30 of 36 point estimates negative. Best-of-N with self-verify vs counting the same 8 samples: counting better by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B but only 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B (CIs include zero). Self-consistency 1.5B GSM8K: 70.1% (297 tokens) to 80.9% (4749 tokens). A forced Reflexion variant on the smallest model never triggered a retry on its own.
limits: Math with one checkable answer, not hypothesis revision with new data. Small open models only (no frontier). Single author, preprint, question variance only (no run variance). Majority vote does not apply to open-ended causal hypotheses, so the equal-cost baseline for blicket is different (for example N independent full runs plus a consistency check).
agent_relevance: A REVISE loop that re-reads its own earlier answer should be tested against N independent tries at equal tokens before it is trusted. Revising against new external data (a test result) is not covered by this result.

source: Leins, Pelleriti, Gonnermann-Muller, Pokutta (2026) When Does LLM Orchestration Pay Off? A Controlled Evaluation of Accuracy, Cost, and Task Difficulty
finding: Self-Refine, Best-of-N and Debate, each tuned with the same optimiser budget (GEPA), on five LLM backbones. Gains over single-call chain-of-thought are small, depend on the benchmark and the model, and cost 2-4 times the tokens.
numbers: 3 domains (competitive programming, chess puzzles, math), 5 backbones. Largest average gain over optimised CoT 4.6 points (4.5 over task-only). Adding method to a mixed model: Codeforces chi2(3)=18.62, p=.0003; AMC chi2(3)=13.76, p=.0032; Lichess chi2(3)=4.34, p=.227. Gains did not grow with item difficulty. Strong method-by-backbone interaction.
limits: No blicket or causal task. Compares to single-call baselines, not to repeated sampling at equal tokens. 2026 backbones, mix of closed and open models.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that loop gains are model-specific. Pick the REVISE test model; do not assume transfer.

source: Beckers, Vandorpe, Debeys, De Houwer (2009) Three-year-olds' retrospective revaluation in the blicket detector task (Experimental Psychology 56:27)
finding: A test of the Sobel et al. 2004 backward-blocking result in younger children. Three-year-olds showed recovery from overshadowing but NO backward blocking. The authors say this is consistent with inferential and computational models of causal learning.
numbers: No numbers: only the Crossref abstract was read; the paper was not opened.
limits: Abstract only (opened false). Three-year-olds are younger than the 4-year-olds in Sobel 2004, so it is a boundary rather than a pure failed replication.
agent_relevance: Retroactive discounting is not a free ability, even in children. Do not assume an LLM does it. Test it by re-scoring old evidence after a later observation.

source: Forward and backward blocking in statistical learning (PLoS One 2024; preprint 2022)
finding: Adults in an incidental statistical-learning task, with reaction times as the measure. Backward blocking was found: the blocked stimulus showed no expectation effect while control did. Forward blocking was NOT found (the blocked stimulus showed more effect than control).
numbers: Exp 1 forward blocking: 92 recruited, 42 excluded (accuracy below 80%), 50 kept. Exp 2 backward blocking: 84 recruited, 50 kept. Exp 2 RT expected vs unexpected: companion 477 vs 487 ms (dz=0.35); control 491 vs 501 (dz=0.39); blocked 496 vs 496 ms (dz=-0.01); interaction b=9.45, 95% CI [1.34, 17.63], dz=0.32. Explicit pair knowledge 50-59%, near chance for blocked.
limits: Not a causal-reasoning task: learning was incidental and effects were under 20 ms. Many exclusions. The authors say backward blocking is harder to obtain than forward blocking and may reflect test-phase performance rather than learning. Only the first 100,000 characters of 139,368 were read.
agent_relevance: Mixed adult evidence: backward blocking appears in some low-level tasks and fails in others (Benton and Rakison). Gap 5 stays open for explicit causal rating tasks and for LLMs.

source: Zhang, Jia, Edmonds, Zhu, Zhu (2021) ACRE: Abstract Causal REasoning Beyond Covariation (CVPR)
finding: Pre-LLM test of backward-blocking and screening-off queries in a visual blicket benchmark. Pure neural models learn covariation (up to 87% on indirect queries) but fail screening-off and backward-blocking queries.
numbers: 30,000 problems; four query types (direct, indirect, screening-off, backward-blocking). The backward-blocking row in the first split of Table 2 spans 23.91% to 99.80% across ten models (column labels were not read, so which model is which is unknown).
limits: Visual models, not LLMs; 2021. Model-to-number mapping not read. Not evidence about current LLMs.
agent_relevance: Backward blocking is the hardest query type: a good probe for S5 revision, since it needs the agent to lower belief in B because of a later test of A.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of LMs with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR 2024) - ablation re-read
finding: No refine-vs-sampling comparison at equal tokens in this paper. A related ablation shows that self-consistency (N=5) and zero-shot chain-of-thought do not help rule application. Zero-shot CoT hurts on ACRE.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy: standard 77.8, 0-CoT 73.2, SC(N=5) 77.0. ACRE task accuracy: 47.0, 25.0, 46.0. The cost table lists API calls and is not matched against sampling.
limits: 2023-era GPT-4 and GPT-3.5. The refine gain (c20, ACRE 64.0 to 82.5) comes with a symbolic interpreter, which is different from LLM self-revision.
agent_relevance: Keeps K12 weak: the refinement gain depends on an external checker, not on the loop. At S5 give the agent a mechanical check of hypothesis against data.

source: Gopnik and Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism (Psych Bull) - re-read for the original numbers
finding: Tried to recover primary numbers for Gopnik 2001, Sobel 2004 and Denison 2010 through the best open review. It does not have them. It names ages (2-, 3-, 4-year-olds for Gopnik 2001; preschoolers for Sobel 2004) and gives no N or test statistic. The Denison 2010 80/20 chip figure is a hypothetical example, not a reported result. Sobel and Kirkham 2007 is 18-month-olds (backward blocking); no numbers on the page.
numbers: The only exact numbers in the part read are false-belief figures (Liu et al. 2007: almost 50 preschoolers, 65% passed over 75% of tasks, 30% passed under 25%). No failed replications reported in this review.
limits: Read characters 0-100,000 of 222,442. The originals (Developmental Psychology 37:620; Cognitive Science 28:303) are behind a paywall (HTTP 403 from Wiley, APA redirect), and no free copy was found in the time available.
agent_relevance: The numbers behind K01 stay second-hand. Do not quote the Denison chip numbers as data.

source: arXiv search listings, 31 Oct 2026: blicket; backward blocking; retrospective revaluation; explaining away; pedagogy narrowing in LLM agents
finding: Negative search results for gaps 5 and 9. A search for 'blicket' lists 9 papers (2019-2026): Samiei 2026, Alderete 2026, Jhaveri 2026, GX-Chen 2025, three 2022 benchmark papers, ACRE 2021 and one unrelated compositional-generalisation paper. 'Backward blocking' returns only ACRE as relevant (the other hits are unrelated physics and numerics). 'Retrospective revaluation language models' returns one unrelated paper. 'Explaining away LLM causal learning children' returns nothing. A search for instruction narrowing LLM exploration returns nothing. Two later queries were rate-limited (HTTP 429).
numbers: 9 'blicket' results; 0 LLM backward-blocking studies; 0 LLM pedagogy-narrowing studies found.
limits: Keyword search on titles and abstracts only; misses papers that use other words (for example 'retroactive', 'belief revision', 'anchoring'). The web-search tool, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were out of quota, so coverage is thin. Absence here is weak evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 9 have no LLM data in what we could find. Both are tests to run, not claims to rely on.

source: Gap 3 check: outside replications of Alderete et al. and Jhaveri et al. (arXiv listings and citing papers, Oct 2026)
finding: No outside lab has repeated the Alderete scaffold on another model. For Jhaveri, FALSIFYBENCH (different lab, different domain) supports the same link between negative testing and success but did not test a counterexample prompt, so the intervention itself has no outside replication. Jhaveri, GX-Chen 2025 and Samiei 2026 share authors (GX-Chen, Samiei, Gopnik), so the blicket-LLM literature is one connected group, not independent labs.
numbers: Count: Alderete outside replications 0; Jhaveri intervention outside replications 0; Jhaveri correlation corroborated by 1 outside lab (rho=-0.779, 12 models, 100 games each).
limits: Based on arXiv listings and reference lists I could reach. Papers not indexed under these terms would be missed.
agent_relevance: Treat counterexample prompt and context-graph gains as single-lab until our own schema test repeats them.
